title: Identify the Stressor
description: Notice what situation triggers your stressful thought.
steps: Write down the specific situation.
Notice how your body feels.
Write the literal thought as if it was a quote.

title: Spotting All-or-Nothing
description: Find shades of grey in your thinking.
steps: Write your absolute thought (e.g. ruined, always, never).
List one exception to this rule.
Rewrite the thought to include 'sometimes' or 'partially'.

title: 5-4-3-2-1 Technique
description: Use your senses to anchor yourself in the present.
steps: Acknowledge 5 things you see.
Acknowledge 4 things you can touch.
Acknowledge 3 things you hear.
Acknowledge 2 things you smell.
Acknowledge 1 thing you can taste.

title: Box Breathing
description: Calm your nervous system with measured breaths.
steps: Breathe in for 4 seconds.
Hold for 4 seconds.
Exhale for 4 seconds.
Hold empty for 4 seconds.
Repeat 5 times.

title: Three Good Things
description: Shift focus to positives from today.
steps: Write down one good thing.
Write down a second good thing.
Write down a third good thing.
Reflect on how these make you feel.

title: Inner Friend
description: Talk to yourself as you would a friend.
steps: Write down your self-critical thought.
Imagine a dear friend having this thought.
Write down what you would tell them.
Read those words back to yourself.

title: Do One Small Thing
description: Break the cycle of avoidance.
steps: Pick a task that takes under 5 minutes.
Set a timer for 5 minutes.
Do the task immediately.
Check in on your mood afterwards.

title: Imaginal Exposure
description: Visualize a mildly anxiety-provoking scenario.
steps: Sit somewhere safe.
Close your eyes and imagine the scenario.
Rate your anxiety 1-10.
Breathe until it drops by 2 points.

title: Challenge the Thought
description: Examine a recurring negative belief.
steps: Identify the negative belief.
Ask: Is it 100% true?
Ask: What would I tell a friend?
Reframe the thought.

title: Mind Reading Check
description: Stop assuming you know what others think.
steps: Notice who you are mind-reading.
List alternative reasons for their behavior.
Remind yourself you cannot read minds.

title: Color Focus
description: Ground yourself visually by finding colors.
steps: Pick a color.
Find 5 objects of that color in the room.
Describe each object out loud.
Pick another color and repeat.

title: Progressive Relaxation
description: Release tension from your muscles.
steps: Tense your toes for 5 seconds.
Release and notice the relaxation.
Move up to your calves, tense and release.
Continue moving up your body to your face.

title: Appreciation Letter
description: Express gratitude mentally or in writing.
steps: Think of someone who helped you.
Write a short paragraph of what they did.
Notice any warm feelings in your chest.

title: Forgiveness Practice
description: Let go of a small mistake.
steps: Acknowledge the mistake without judgment.
Remind yourself everyone makes mistakes.
Take a deep breath and visualize letting it go.

title: Pleasant Activity Scheduling
description: Plan a small enjoyment.
steps: Brainstorm 3 simple things you enjoy.
Pick one to do today.
Schedule an exact time.
Do it.

title: Worry Time
description: Confine worry to a specific block of time.
steps: Schedule 15 minutes of 'worry time'.
During the day, jot down worries and postpone them.
When the time comes, review the list.
When time is up, stop and do another activity.

title: Examine the Evidence
description: Look at facts objectively.
steps: Write down the belief.
List evidence that supports it.
List evidence against it.
Incorporate both into a balanced thought.

title: Label Reducer
description: Change global labels to specific behaviors.
steps: Catch yourself calling yourself a name.
Identify the specific behavior you regret.
Acknowledge that one behavior doesn't define you.

title: Texture Walk
description: Focus on the physical sensation of touch.
steps: Find an object near you.
Feel its texture with your fingertips.
Describe the texture (smooth, rough, cold).
Find a second object and compare.

title: Shoulder Drop
description: Release physical tension held in your shoulders.
steps: Notice if your shoulders are raised.
Take a deep breath in.
Exhale forcibly while dropping shoulders.
Roll them back twice.

title: Silver Linings
description: Find one positive in a neutral or negative situation.
steps: Pick a minor annoyance from today.
Find one small silver lining in it.
Focus on that silver lining for 30 seconds.

title: Soothing Touch
description: Provide yourself with physical comfort.
steps: Place a hand over your heart or on your arm.
Feel the warmth of your hand.
Take three deep, slow breaths.

title: Routine Anchor
description: Attach a new habit to an existing one.
steps: Identify something you do every day (like brushing teeth).
Choose a 2-minute positive action.
Do them together.

title: Decatastrophize a Fear
description: Examine the feared outcome.
steps: Write down what you fear will happen.
Write down how you would survive it.
Write down a more realistic outcome.

title: De-catastrophizing
description: Manage worst-case scenario thinking.
steps: Identify the worst-case scenario.
Estimate how likely it really is.
Imagine how you would cope if it happened.
Identify the best-case scenario.

title: Should Statements
description: Replace 'should' with 'would like'.
steps: Write down a 'should' statement.
Change it to 'I would prefer' or 'It would be nice if'.
Notice how the pressure changes.

title: Temperature Notice
description: Use temperature to ground your body.
steps: Hold an ice cube or something cold.
Focus entirely on the cold sensation.
Notice how your hand feels as it warns up.

title: 4-7-8 Breathing
description: A relaxing breath pattern.
steps: Inhale quietly through your nose for 4 seconds.
Hold the breath for 7 seconds.
Exhale completely through your mouth for 8 seconds.
Repeat 4 times.

title: Future Gratitude
description: Look forward to something positive.
steps: Think of one thing happening tomorrow to enjoy.
Visualize it.
Write down why you are looking forward to it.

title: Shared Humanity
description: Remember you are not alone.
steps: Notice a feeling of inadequacy.
Remind yourself that thousands feel this right now.
Acknowledge that struggling is part of being human.

title: Mastery Task
description: Do something that gives a sense of accomplishment.
steps: Pick a task you've been putting off.
Break it into an incredibly small first step.
Complete just that first step.

title: Safety Behavior Drop
description: Gradually remove crutches.
steps: Identify something you do just to feel 'safe'.
Try doing the activity without it once.
Notice that you survived without the safety behavior.

title: STOP Skill
description: A DBT-inspired pause for intense moments. This is an educational self-help exercise, not therapy or medical advice.
steps: Stop. Pause what you are doing and avoid making the moment bigger.
Take a step back. Put both feet on the floor, breathe out slowly, or create a little physical space.
Observe. Name what is happening around you, what you feel in your body, and what thoughts are showing up.
Proceed mindfully. Choose one small next action that fits your values and keeps things steady.
completionSummary: You practiced creating space between a strong feeling and your next action.
journalReflection: What changed after you paused before responding?

title: TIPP Skill
description: A DBT-inspired body reset for moments that feel very intense. Skip any part that feels unsafe for your body; this is self-help education, not medical advice.
steps: Temperature: hold something cool, splash cool water on your face, or step near fresh air for a brief reset.
Intense movement: move for 30 to 60 seconds in a way that is safe for you, such as brisk walking, wall push-ups, or marching in place.
Paced breathing: breathe out longer than you breathe in for one minute.
Paired muscle release: gently tense one muscle group for five seconds, then relax it and notice the difference.
completionSummary: You tried body-based skills to lower the intensity enough to choose your next step.
journalReflection: Which part of TIPP felt most helpful or least helpful today?

title: Wise Mind Check-In
description: A DBT-inspired check-in that helps you listen to both feelings and facts before choosing a response.
steps: Name the feeling mind: what emotion is loudest right now?
Name the reasonable mind: what facts do you know for sure?
Imagine both sides sitting at the same table instead of arguing.
Ask: what would a balanced, grounded next step look like?
Write one sentence that starts with: Wise mind says...
completionSummary: You practiced balancing emotion and facts before deciding what to do next.
journalReflection: What did your wise mind notice that one side alone might have missed?

title: Check the Facts
description: A DBT-inspired way to compare a strong emotion with the facts of the situation.
steps: Write the event in plain words, like a camera recording only what happened.
Name the emotion and rate its intensity from 1 to 10.
List the facts that support the emotion.
List facts that do not fit the emotion or point to another explanation.
Ask: does the emotion fit the facts, or is it asking for a smaller response?
completionSummary: You separated facts from interpretations and checked whether the emotion matched the situation.
journalReflection: Which fact was easiest to miss at first?

title: Opposite Action
description: A DBT-inspired practice for choosing a small action that goes against an unhelpful urge. Do not use this to ignore real danger, personal limits, or values.
steps: Name the emotion and the urge it brings, such as hiding, snapping, quitting, or avoiding.
Check whether the urge fits the facts and your values.
If the urge is not helping, choose one small opposite action.
Make the action specific: where, when, and for how long?
Try the action for a short amount of time and notice what shifts.
completionSummary: You practiced acting from intention instead of automatically following an unhelpful urge.
journalReflection: What did you learn from doing the opposite action, even briefly?

title: Urge Surfing
description: A DBT-inspired exercise for riding out an urge without judging it or acting on it right away.
steps: Name the urge in simple words: I am noticing the urge to...
Rate the urge from 1 to 10.
Picture the urge as a wave that rises, peaks, and falls.
Track where you feel it in your body for one minute.
Choose a safe delay, such as five minutes, then rate the urge again.
completionSummary: You observed an urge as something that changes over time, rather than a command you have to follow.
journalReflection: What helped you stay with the urge while it moved through?

title: Self-Soothe With the Five Senses
description: A DBT-inspired grounding practice that uses everyday sensory comfort to settle the moment.
steps: Sight: choose something calming or pleasant to look at for 30 seconds.
Sound: listen for one steady sound, quiet song, or gentle background noise.
Smell: notice a comforting scent, fresh air, soap, tea, or another safe smell.
Taste: take one mindful sip or bite and describe it slowly.
Touch: use a blanket, warm mug, smooth object, or steady hand pressure to add comfort.
completionSummary: You used the five senses to bring small, concrete comfort into the present moment.
journalReflection: Which sense gave you the strongest feeling of steadiness?

title: PLEASE Skill Reflection
description: A DBT-inspired reflection on everyday body basics that can affect mood. This is not medical advice; follow professional guidance for health needs.
steps: Physical care: note one basic need your body has today, such as rest, food, water, movement, or medication as already prescribed.
Eating: ask whether you have eaten in a way that supports your energy today.
Avoid mood-altering extras: notice whether substances, too much caffeine, or other choices are affecting you.
Sleep: write one small thing that could make tonight easier.
Exercise: choose one realistic movement option, even a short walk or stretch.
completionSummary: You reviewed practical body basics that can make emotions easier to manage.
journalReflection: Which basic need deserves a little attention today?

title: Distress Tolerance Plan
description: A DBT-inspired plan for getting through a hard moment without making it worse. If you might harm yourself or someone else, seek urgent help now.
steps: Write one early warning sign that tells you distress is rising.
Choose three safe skills you can try first, such as STOP, paced breathing, self-soothing, or stepping away.
List two people, places, or supports that help you stay grounded.
Name one action to avoid because it usually makes things worse.
Write a simple plan: When I notice distress rising, I will...
completionSummary: You created a simple plan for moving through distress with fewer regrets.
journalReflection: What support or skill would be easiest to use when things feel intense?

title: Emotion Regulation Review
description: A DBT-inspired review for understanding what shaped an emotion and what helped you respond.
steps: Pick one emotion from today and name it without judging it.
Write what prompted the emotion.
Notice body clues, thoughts, urges, and actions that came with it.
Identify one skill or choice that helped even a little.
Choose one small adjustment for next time.
completionSummary: You reviewed an emotion with curiosity and identified one useful adjustment for the future.
journalReflection: What did this emotion seem to need from you?

title: Values Clarification
description: Name what matters to you so your next choice can point in that direction.
steps: Pick one life area: relationships, health, learning, work, community, or rest.
Ask: What kind of person do I want to be here?
Write three values, such as kindness, honesty, courage, care, or patience.
Choose one value that feels important this week.
Name one small action that could show that value today.
completionSummary: You named a value and one small way to live it.
journalReflection: Which value felt most alive today, and what could you do next?

title: Values Compass
description: Check which valued directions need more attention right now.
steps: Draw or imagine a compass with four directions: care, growth, connection, and health.
Rate each direction from 0 to 10 for how closely your actions match your values.
Pick the lowest score that still matters to you.
Write one barrier that pulls you off course.
Choose one small action to move one point closer.
completionSummary: You checked your values compass and chose one small move forward.
journalReflection: Which direction needs a little more care this week?

title: Cognitive Defusion: "I'm Having the Thought That..."
description: Practice seeing thoughts as words in your mind, not facts you must obey.
steps: Write one sticky thought in a short sentence.
Add these words before it: I'm having the thought that...
Say the new sentence slowly.
Add another layer: I notice I'm having the thought that...
Ask: Does holding this thought lightly help me move toward what matters?
completionSummary: You practiced holding a thought more lightly.
journalReflection: How did the thought feel when you added distance from it?

title: Leaves on a Stream
description: Let thoughts come and go without needing to push them away.
steps: Sit comfortably and notice your breathing.
Picture a slow stream with leaves floating by.
When a thought shows up, place it on a leaf.
Let the leaf float past at its own speed.
If you get pulled into a thought, gently return to the stream.
completionSummary: You practiced noticing thoughts and letting them move through.
journalReflection: What thoughts kept returning, and how did you respond to them?

title: Control vs Influence
description: Sort a hard situation into what you can control, influence, and let be.
steps: Write the situation in one sentence.
List what is directly in your control, such as your words or next step.
List what you may influence but cannot force.
List what is outside your control.
Choose one useful action from the control or influence list.
completionSummary: You separated control, influence, and things to let be.
journalReflection: What changed when you focused on one useful action?

title: Acceptance Practice
description: Practice allowing a feeling to be present while you stay kind to yourself.
steps: Name the feeling in simple words.
Notice where it shows up in your body.
Say: This feeling is here right now.
Breathe slowly and soften around the feeling if you can.
Choose one gentle action that fits your values.
completionSummary: You practiced making space for a feeling without needing to fight it.
journalReflection: What helped you allow the feeling to be there?

title: Committed Action Plan
description: Turn a value into a small, realistic next step.
steps: Choose one value you want to act on.
Name one action that is small enough to do this week.
Set a time and place for the action.
Name one obstacle that may show up.
Choose a backup step that is even smaller.
Afterward, mark what you did and what you learned.
completionSummary: You made a clear plan for one values-based action.
journalReflection: What would make this action easier to start?

title: Self-as-Context Reflection
description: Notice that you are more than one thought, feeling, or role.
steps: Write: I am noticing...
Add one thought, one feeling, and one body sensation.
Ask: Who is noticing these experiences?
Rest for a few breaths as the observer of the experience.
Write: I can notice this and still choose my next step.
completionSummary: You practiced noticing experiences from a steadier point of view.
journalReflection: What did you notice when you stepped back from the experience?

title: Passengers on the Bus
description: See difficult thoughts and feelings as passengers while you choose the direction.
steps: Imagine you are driving a bus toward something that matters.
Name the passengers that show up, such as fear, doubt, shame, or anger.
Let each passenger speak without arguing with it.
Thank them for trying to protect you.
Keep your hands on the wheel and choose one small move forward.
completionSummary: You practiced making room for inner passengers while keeping your direction.
journalReflection: Which passenger was loudest, and what direction still mattered?

title: Making Room for Feelings
description: Make space for a feeling instead of spending all your energy fighting it.
steps: Name the feeling.
Picture how much space it takes up.
Breathe around it, as if making the space a little wider.
Unclench your jaw, shoulders, or hands if you can.
Say: I can make room for this and still do what matters.
completionSummary: You practiced making room for a feeling and choosing what matters.
journalReflection: What became possible when you made a little room for the feeling?

title: 3-Minute Breathing Space
description: A compact practice for pausing, breathing, and returning to the next moment with steadier attention.
steps: Minute 1: Notice what is here right now, including thoughts, emotions, and body sensations.
Minute 2: Gather your attention around the natural rhythm of breathing.
Minute 3: Expand awareness to the whole body, the room, and the next small action.
completionSummary: You practiced shifting from automatic pilot into a steadier, more spacious awareness.
journalReflection: What changed between the first minute and the final minute?

title: Body Scan
description: Move attention through the body to notice sensation, tension, warmth, or numbness without needing to fix it.
steps: Settle into a comfortable position and let your breathing be natural.
Bring attention to your feet and notice any sensations there.
Slowly move attention through legs, hips, belly, chest, hands, arms, shoulders, neck, and face.
When the mind wanders, gently name 'wandering' and return to the next body area.
End by sensing the whole body breathing as one field of awareness.
completionSummary: You trained gentle body awareness and practiced returning attention without judgment.
journalReflection: Where did you notice ease, tension, or surprise in your body?

title: Five Senses Grounding
description: Use sight, touch, sound, smell, and taste to anchor yourself in the here and now.
steps: Name five things you can see, noticing color, shape, or light.
Name four things you can feel through touch or body contact.
Name three sounds you can hear, near or far.
Name two scents you can detect, or two scents you remember clearly.
Name one taste, then take one slow breath and look around again.
completionSummary: You used sensory detail to reconnect with your immediate environment.
journalReflection: Which sense helped you feel most present?

title: Mindful Walking
description: Turn ordinary walking into a practice of attention, rhythm, and contact with the ground.
steps: Choose a short path where you can walk safely without rushing.
Feel each foot lift, move, and make contact with the ground.
Notice the rhythm of breath, movement, and balance.
When attention drifts, return to the sensation of your next step.
Pause at the end and notice how your body feels after moving slowly.
completionSummary: You practiced bringing full attention to movement and physical contact with the world.
journalReflection: What did slowing down reveal about walking that you usually miss?

title: Mindful Eating
description: Use one small bite or sip to practice noticing texture, scent, flavor, and pace.
steps: Choose one bite of food or one sip of a drink.
Look closely at color, shape, and surface before eating.
Notice scent and any anticipation in your body.
Take the bite or sip slowly, tracking texture and flavor as they change.
Pause before the next bite and notice satisfaction, hunger, or habit.
completionSummary: You practiced savoring and noticing the body during a familiar daily activity.
journalReflection: How did attention change the experience of eating or drinking?

title: Noting Thoughts
description: Label thoughts as mental events so they can be noticed without automatically becoming commands.
steps: Sit quietly and let thoughts come and go naturally.
When a thought appears, gently label it 'planning', 'remembering', 'judging', 'worrying', or simply 'thinking'.
Return attention to the breath or body after each label.
If the same thought returns, note it again with a neutral tone.
End by naming one thought pattern you noticed.
completionSummary: You practiced seeing thoughts as passing experiences rather than facts you must obey.
journalReflection: Which thought label showed up most often?

title: Observing Emotions
description: Notice an emotion as a changing body experience with a name, location, and intensity.
steps: Choose one emotion that is present enough to observe safely.
Name the emotion with a simple label, such as sadness, anger, worry, or tenderness.
Find where it shows up in the body and describe the sensations.
Rate its intensity from 1 to 10, then breathe with it for one minute.
Rate it again and note whether it changed, stayed, or moved.
completionSummary: You practiced making room for emotion while tracking it with curiosity.
journalReflection: What did the emotion seem to need from you?

title: Present Moment Anchor
description: Choose one reliable anchor and return to it whenever attention gets pulled away.
steps: Pick an anchor: breath, feet on the floor, hands touching, or a steady sound.
Rest attention on the anchor for three natural breaths.
When attention moves away, silently say 'back' and return to the anchor.
Repeat until the timer ends, letting each return count as the practice.
completionSummary: You strengthened the skill of coming back to the present one return at a time.
journalReflection: Which anchor felt most steady today?

title: Sleep Wind-Down Scan
description: A gentle evening scan for releasing the day and preparing the body for rest.
steps: Lie down or sit comfortably and let your eyes close or soften.
Notice the points where your body is supported.
Scan from forehead to jaw, shoulders, chest, belly, hips, legs, and feet.
At each area, invite a small release on the exhale without forcing relaxation.
End by naming one thing you can set down until tomorrow.
completionSummary: You practiced easing attention out of the day and into physical rest.
journalReflection: What felt ready to be released before sleep?

title: Self-Compassion Pause
description: Pause during a hard moment to acknowledge pain, shared humanity, and one kind response.
steps: Name the difficult moment in plain language: 'This is hard right now.'
Place a hand somewhere comforting, such as your chest, arm, or cheek.
Remind yourself: 'Difficulty is part of being human.'
Ask: 'What is one kind thing I can offer myself in this moment?'
Choose a small supportive action, phrase, or boundary.
completionSummary: You practiced meeting difficulty with acknowledgement and kindness instead of criticism.
journalReflection: What kind phrase or action felt most believable?

title: Three Good Things
description: Record three things that went well and explore what helped them happen.
steps: Write down one good thing from today, even if it was small.
Write a second good thing and name what made it possible.
Write a third good thing and notice your role, another person's role, or good timing.
Pause for one breath with each item before finishing.
completionSummary: You practiced training attention toward moments of goodness, contribution, and support.
journalReflection: Which good thing do you want to remember tomorrow?

title: Best Possible Self
description: Imagine a realistic future where you have moved toward what matters and supported yourself well.
steps: Choose a future time frame, such as six months or one year from now.
Write about yourself handling life in a way that reflects your values.
Include concrete details about relationships, health, work, learning, or daily rhythm.
Identify one strength or habit that helped this future become more likely.
Pick one small action you can take this week in that direction.
completionSummary: You clarified an energizing future and connected it to one practical next step.
journalReflection: What part of this future felt most alive or important?

title: Gratitude Letter
description: Write a specific note of appreciation to someone whose actions mattered to you.
steps: Choose someone who helped, encouraged, taught, or supported you.
Describe what they did in specific detail.
Write how their action affected you then and how it still matters now.
Decide whether to send, read, save, or simply use the letter as private reflection.
Take a moment to notice any warmth, tenderness, or resistance that appears.
completionSummary: You practiced making appreciation specific and visible.
journalReflection: What did writing this letter help you recognize?

title: Savoring a Good Moment
description: Slow down with one pleasant moment so your mind and body have time to register it.
steps: Choose a recent or current good moment, however ordinary.
Replay or observe the sensory details: sights, sounds, textures, smells, and feelings.
Name what made the moment meaningful, enjoyable, or comforting.
Let yourself stay with the good feeling for three slow breaths.
Consider one way to make room for similar moments again.
completionSummary: You practiced extending attention toward a positive experience instead of rushing past it.
journalReflection: What did you notice when you let the good moment last longer?

title: Strengths Spotting
description: Notice strengths in yourself or someone else and connect them to real behavior.
steps: Choose yourself or another person to observe kindly.
Identify one strength shown recently, such as courage, humor, fairness, curiosity, patience, or care.
Write the specific behavior that showed the strength.
Name how that strength affected the situation.
Choose one way to use or appreciate that strength again.
completionSummary: You practiced seeing strengths as observable patterns, not vague compliments.
journalReflection: Which strength do you want to notice more often this week?

title: Kindness Challenge
description: Plan one small act of kindness that is realistic, specific, and freely chosen.
steps: Choose a person, group, or place that could use a small supportive action.
Brainstorm three kind actions that would take ten minutes or less.
Pick one action that fits your energy and boundaries today.
Decide when and how you will do it.
Afterward, notice the effect on you and, if visible, the other person.
completionSummary: You turned kindness into a concrete action while respecting your capacity.
journalReflection: How did choosing or doing the kind action affect your mood?

title: Meaningful Moment Reflection
description: Reflect on a moment that felt meaningful and identify the value it points toward.
steps: Recall one recent moment that felt meaningful, grounding, or important.
Describe what happened without judging whether it was big enough.
Name the value present in the moment, such as care, learning, honesty, courage, beauty, or service.
Notice what the moment says about what matters to you.
Choose one small way to honor that value again.
completionSummary: You connected an ordinary moment to a deeper value that can guide future action.
journalReflection: What value was asking for more attention?

title: Hope Mapping
description: Build hope by naming a goal, pathways toward it, obstacles, and sources of agency.
steps: Write one goal that matters and is realistic enough to influence.
List two or three pathways that could move you toward the goal.
Name one likely obstacle for each pathway.
For each obstacle, write a backup route or support you could use.
Choose the first small step and when you will take it.
completionSummary: You practiced hope as a skill: goals, pathways, flexibility, and agency.
journalReflection: Which pathway feels most workable right now?

title: Accomplishment Log
description: Record small wins to help your brain notice effort, progress, and follow-through.
steps: List three things you did today or recently, including small maintenance tasks.
For each item, name the effort or strength it required.
Notice any task you are tempted to dismiss and write why it still counts.
Choose one accomplishment to acknowledge with a simple phrase: 'That mattered.'
completionSummary: You practiced recognizing progress that may otherwise pass unnoticed.
journalReflection: What accomplishment did you almost overlook?

title: Appreciation Practice
description: Name one person, place, object, or experience you appreciate and let the feeling become specific.
steps: Choose one thing you appreciate right now.
Write three specific qualities, actions, or details you value about it.
Notice how your body responds as you focus on appreciation.
Decide whether to express the appreciation outwardly or simply carry it with you.
Take one slow breath before moving on.
completionSummary: You practiced making appreciation concrete, embodied, and available.
journalReflection: What detail made your appreciation feel real?
